blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A district's best plan spends about 97% of every year's budget. The board adds a floor: every year's budget must be spent in full. What happens to the best plan's NPV?

options.text: It falls, since each year must be filled exactly, valuable work or not
options.says: Right: an exact fill funds work for its cost, not its value; on GridCap small it cost $5,228k.

options.text: It rises, since the unspent money now goes to more valuable projects
options.says: A floor only removes plans, so the best NPV can never rise; the unconstrained plan already chose the best use of the money.

options.text: It stays the same, since the floor reaches only the last 3% of the money
options.says: The last percent forced a reshuffle worth over a fifth of GridCap's NPV; the size of the gap says nothing about the cost.

options.text: It stays the same, since a floor never binds a plan already near its budget
options.says: GridCap's plan spent 98% or more of every year, and a 99% floor already cost $174k.

origin.section: A Spend Limit Is a Row on a Spend Expression, From Above or From Below

questions.stem: Repairs must be at least 25% of what the plan spends. R is the plan's repair spend and S its total spend, both linear expressions of the binaries; B is the budget. Which row states the rule?

options.says: A ratio of two variable expressions is not linear; multiply both sides by S, which is never negative.
That is a fixed floor on repair spend, a share of the budget; it ignores how much the plan really spends.
Right: the ratio rule multiplied out by S, as with min_share_vegetation.
That holds for every plan, since repairs are part of S; it bounds the wrong side.

origin.section: A Share of the Plan Is Linear Once You Multiply Out the Total

questions.stem: Each of five districts has a spend floor below the total cost of its projects (one option per alternative group), and the floors together are below the budgets together. What do these two checks prove?

options.text: That some plan meets every floor and every budget
options.says: GridCap's tripled floors passed both checks and the model was still INFEASIBLE.

options.text: That no floor will bind in the best plan found
options.says: The raised Plains floor passed both checks and changed the plan.

options.text: That the floors cost the plan nothing in NPV
options.says: A floor that passes the checks can still cost NPV: the raised Plains floor cost $423k.

options.text: Only that two causes of infeasibility are absent
options.says: Right: the checks are necessary, not sufficient; windows, yearly budgets and must-dos can still conflict.

origin.section: Floors Can Make the Model Infeasible: Check Them First, Knowing the Checks Are Not Enough
